title: What happens to late events that arrive after the watermark has passed the window's end — they are dropped by default, or handled via allowed lateness (window stays open longer) or side outputs (late events routed to a separate stream for special handling)?
shortTitle: What happens to late events in Flink

s1_definition.profdef: A late event in Flink is a record whose event-time timestamp falls into a window that has already fired because the watermark has moved past that window's end. By default Flink silently drops late events. You can instead give a window a period of allowed lateness, during which the window state is retained and each late event triggers a recomputation and re-emission of the window result. For events later than even the allowed-lateness period, you can attach a side output so those records are routed to a separate stream for special handling rather than being lost.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India closes the books for the 10:00-to-10:01 minute once the manager announces that minute is over. If Rajesh's transaction that happened at 10:00:30 arrives a little after closing, the bank has three choices. By default, the clerk shrugs and throws the slip away, so it is simply lost. With allowed lateness, the bank keeps that minute's ledger page open for an extra two minutes and, if the slip arrives within that grace period, reopens the page, adds the amount, and reprints the corrected total. If the slip arrives even later than the grace period, the bank does not lose it either; it drops the slip into a special "late arrivals" tray (the side output) so a human can reconcile it manually.
s1_definition.oneliner: Late events are dropped by default, kept and recomputed if within allowed lateness, and captured in a side output if you route them there.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A late event in Flink is a record whose event-time timestamp falls into a window that has already fired because the watermark has moved past that window's end. By default Flink silently drops late events. You can instead give a window a period of allowed lateness, during which the window state is retained and each late event triggers a recomputation and re-emission of the window result. For events later than even the allowed-lateness period, you can attach a side output so those records are routed to a separate stream for special handling rather than being lost.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India closes the books for the 10:00-to-10:01 minute once the manager announces that minute is over. If Rajesh's transaction that happened at 10:00:30 arrives a little after closing, the bank has three choices. By default, the clerk shrugs and throws the slip away, so it is simply lost. With allowed lateness, the bank keeps that minute's ledger page open for an extra two minutes and, if the slip arrives within that grace period, reopens the page, adds the amount, and reprints the corrected total. If the slip arrives even later than the grace period, the bank does not lose it either; it drops the slip into a special "late arrivals" tray (the side output) so a human can reconcile it manually.

**One line to remember:** Late events are dropped by default, kept and recomputed if within allowed lateness, and captured in a side output if you route them there.

sections.s2_technical:
A window fires when the watermark crosses its end time. Any event whose timestamp belongs to that window but arrives after the watermark has passed is late. The default behavior is that Flink drops these late events without any error, which is efficient but silently loses data. For many correctness-sensitive jobs that silent loss is unacceptable, so Flink gives you two layered tools.

The first tool is allowed lateness, configured per window with `.allowedLateness(Time.minutes(2))`. With allowed lateness the window does not purge its state immediately when it first fires. Instead it keeps the state for the extra lateness period. During that grace period, every late event that still belongs to the window triggers the window function again and emits an updated result. This means downstream consumers may see the window result more than once: once at the first firing, then an updated value for each late arrival. Your downstream sink must therefore be idempotent or upsert-capable, because it will receive corrections. Once the watermark passes the window end plus the allowed lateness, the state is finally purged.

The second tool is side outputs, configured with `.sideOutputLateData(lateTag)` where `lateTag` is an `OutputTag`. Events later than the allowed-lateness window are not dropped; they are emitted to the side stream identified by that tag. You then retrieve the side stream with `result.getSideOutput(lateTag)` and process it separately, for example writing it to a reconciliation topic, raising an alert, or persisting it for a nightly manual review. The senior nuance is that these two tools combine: a small allowed lateness handles the common slightly-late case automatically with recomputation, and a side output catches the rare very-late case for human or batch handling. The right allowed-lateness value is a business decision balancing correctness against how long you keep window state in memory and how many re-emissions downstream can tolerate.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India computes a per-account one-minute transaction total used by the fraud engine. Transactions are event-time stamped and mostly arrive within a few seconds, but a small fraction arrive slightly late because of mobile retries. If those slightly-late transactions are dropped, the per-minute total is understated and the fraud engine might miss a genuine burst. We want the window to stay open a little longer and correct itself when a slightly-late transaction arrives. This is exactly allowed lateness: the window keeps its state for a short grace period and re-emits an updated total for each late arrival.

Problem 2 — Occasionally a transaction arrives very late, for example an hour later because the merchant's terminal was offline. We cannot keep every window open for an hour, that would blow up memory, and we should not drop the transaction either, because it still represents real money that must be reconciled. We want to capture these very-late transactions in a separate stream for the reconciliation team. This is exactly a side output: anything later than the allowed-lateness grace period is routed to a dedicated late-data stream instead of being lost.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo reproducing all three behaviors. We create a `Txn` record with an event time. A `LateAwareWindowEngine` maintains per-minute windows with a configurable watermark, an allowed-lateness grace period, and a side-output list. When an event arrives it classifies it as on-time (accepted normally), late-but-within-grace (window reopened and re-emitted), or too-late (routed to the side output). A `LateEventsDemo` main class feeds a stream containing one on-time transaction, one slightly-late transaction that triggers a recomputation, and one very-late transaction that lands in the side output, printing each outcome.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  late:
    window-seconds: 60
    out-of-orderness-seconds: 5
    allowed-lateness-seconds: 120   # grace period for recomputation
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five transactions with a one-minute window, five-second out-of-orderness, and two-minute allowed lateness. The key window under study is the 10:00 window for Rajesh (SAV2001).

Step 1: Rajesh transacts 1000 rupees at event time 10 seconds. The max seen is 10 seconds, watermark minus five equals 5 seconds, which is far below the 10:00 window end of 60 seconds. The event is on time, so it is accepted and the 10:00 window total for Rajesh becomes 1000.

Step 2: Priya transacts 500 rupees at event time 120 seconds. This advances the max seen to 120 seconds and the watermark to 115 seconds, which is now well past the 10:00 window end of 60 seconds. The 10:00 window has effectively fired.

Step 3: A slightly-late Rajesh transaction of 250 rupees stamped at 30 seconds arrives. Its window is 10:00, whose end is 60 seconds. The watermark is 115 seconds, which is past 60 but still within 60 plus the 120-second grace, which is 180 seconds. So this is late but within allowed lateness. The window reopens, the total recomputes to 1250, and a corrected result is re-emitted.

Step 4: Priya transacts 700 rupees at event time 600 seconds. The max seen jumps to 600 seconds and the watermark to 595 seconds. This is now past the 10:00 window end plus grace, which is 180 seconds, so the 10:00 window is purged and will no longer accept corrections.

Step 5: A very-late Rajesh transaction of 999 rupees stamped at 40 seconds arrives. Its window is 10:00, but the watermark of 595 seconds is far beyond the 180-second grace limit, and the window is purged. The engine does not drop it silently; it routes the 999 rupees to the side output so the reconciliation team can handle it manually.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] ON-TIME SAV2001|0 total now 1000.00
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] ON-TIME CUR3001|120000 total now 500.00
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [WARNING] LATE-RECOMPUTE SAV2001|0 updated total 1250.00
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] ON-TIME CUR3001|600000 total now 700.00
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [SEVERE] TOO-LATE SAV2001|0 amount 999.00 -> side output
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Final windows = {SAV2001|0=1250.00, CUR3001|120000=500.00, CUR3001|600000=700.00}
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Side-output size = 1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Transaction (event-time stamped)
    │
    ▼
  LateAwareWindowEngine  (window 60s, lateness 120s)
    │ compute watermark = maxSeen - 5s
    │
    ├─ watermark < windowEnd ──────────────→ ON-TIME: add to window, emit
    │
    ├─ windowEnd <= watermark              ──→ LATE-WITHIN-GRACE:
    │  watermark < windowEnd+lateness          reopen window, recompute,
    │                                           RE-EMIT corrected total
    │                                           (downstream must be upsert)
    │
    └─ watermark >= windowEnd+lateness     ──→ TOO-LATE:
                                               route to SIDE OUTPUT stream
                                               → reconciliation topic
    ▼
  Fraud engine reads corrected per-minute totals
  Reconciliation team reads side-output stream
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Late Event Handling Engine ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ State Pattern: window moves OPEN → GRACE → PURGED             │
  │   WHY: each state accepts events differently                  │
  │ Strategy Pattern: classify on-time / late-grace / too-late    │
  │   WHY: isolate the lateness decision from the aggregation     │

  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: engine only classifies+aggregates; sinks handle delivery   │
  │ O: new lateness policy = new branch, sinks unchanged          │
  │ L: any sink consuming side output works the same              │
  │ I: narrow getWindows() / getLateSideOutput() views            │
  │ D: downstream depends on streams, not engine internals        │

  │──────────────────────────────│
  │ + process(Txn): void         │
  │ - windowStart(ts): long      │
  │ - watermark(): long          │
  │ - purgeExpired(wm): void     │
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │ aggregates ◇

         │ Txn          │
         │ + accountId  │
         │ + amount     │
         │ + eventTime  │
         └──────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Window Lateness Lifecycle ──────────────────

  [OPEN] ──wm>=end──→ [GRACE] ──wm>=end+lateness──→ [PURGED]
    │                   │                              │
    │ accept normally   │ accept + recompute + emit    │ route to
    │                   │                              │ side output
    ▼                   ▼                              ▼
  add to total     corrected total               reconciliation

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ────────────────────────────────

  1. engine.process(txn@30s)   // slightly late
  2.   → maxSeen=120000, watermark=115000
  3.   → windowStart=0, end=60000, grace end=180000
  4.   → 60000 <= 115000 < 180000 → LATE-RECOMPUTE
  5.   → windows["SAV2001|0"] 1000 + 250 = 1250, re-emit
  6. engine.process(txn@40s)   // very late, after purge
  7.   → watermark=595000 >= 180000 → side output add
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A late event in Flink is a record whose event-time timestamp belongs to a window that has already fired because the watermark has moved past that window's end. The default behavior is that Flink silently drops late events, which is efficient but means you lose data without any error, and for correctness-sensitive work that is usually unacceptable. Flink gives you two layered tools to handle lateness properly. The first is allowed lateness, where you tell the window to keep its state for an extra grace period after it first fires. During that grace period, every late event that still belongs to the window triggers the window function again and re-emits an updated result, so the window corrects itself. The important consequence is that downstream consumers will see the window result more than once, so the sink must be idempotent or upsert-capable to absorb corrections. Once the watermark passes the window end plus the allowed lateness, the state is finally purged.

The second tool is side outputs. Events that arrive later than even the allowed-lateness period are not dropped; you attach an output tag and Flink routes those very-late records to a separate side stream, which you consume independently to persist them, alert on them, or send them to a reconciliation process. In practice you combine both: a modest allowed lateness handles the common slightly-late case automatically with recomputation, and a side output safely catches the rare very-late case for special handling. The key engineering tradeoff is that allowed lateness keeps window state in memory longer and causes re-emissions, so you tune it to a business-justified value rather than making it arbitrarily large.

At the National Bank of India this mattered directly for our per-account per-minute totals feeding the fraud engine. Most transactions arrived within seconds, but mobile retries meant a small fraction came a little late, so we set a two-minute allowed lateness and made the downstream sink an upsert, which meant a slightly-late transaction would reopen the minute, recompute the total, and push a corrected value so the fraud math stayed accurate. For the rare transaction that arrived an hour late because a merchant terminal had been offline, we could not keep windows open that long, so we attached a side output that routed those records to a dedicated reconciliation topic where the operations team settled them against the ledger. That layered approach, default drop replaced by a tuned allowed lateness for the common case and a side output for the extreme case, is exactly how you get both low latency and no silent data loss in a financial stream.
